scenes.say: Anyone can type any email. So how does your server know who's calling? By the end you'll read a token, store passwords safely, and stop one client flooding your API.

lines.text: Then: how much may they call?

scenes.say: Today you will do three things. Store passwords and read a token. Log in with Google safely. And stop one client flooding your API.
lines: Stop one client flooding your API

scenes.title: How do we store passwords?
scenes.statement: Users sign up with passwords. If the database leaks, nobody's password should leak with it.

example.output: a stored value nobody can reverse

scenes.say: Here's the problem. Users sign up with passwords, and the database may leak one day. For example, the password hunter two. We want to store something nobody can turn back into it.

scenes.head: A hash is a meat grinder
scenes.say: Start with passwords. Never store them. Think of beef, a meat grinder, and mince. Nobody turns mince back into beef. A hash works the same: no way back. At login, grind what they typed, and compare.

scenes.head: Sign up, then log in
scenes.say: Sign up. We feed hunter two to b crypt. Out comes one string, with four parts. Algorithm, b crypt. Cost twelve, meaning two to the twelfth rounds. A random salt, fresh for every user. And the hash itself. At login, we take the salt from that string, hash the typed password again, and compare. Same hash: match.

scenes.head: bcrypt in Python
scenes.say: In Python. Hash the same password twice, each with a fresh salt. Print the first seven characters: algorithm and cost. The two hashes differ, yet check password says true. The salt follows, inside the same string.

panels.code:
pw = b"hunter2"
h1 = bcrypt.hashpw(pw, bcrypt.gensalt(12))
h2 = bcrypt.hashpw(pw, bcrypt.gensalt(12))
print(h1.decode()[:7])
print(h1 != h2, bcrypt.checkpw(pw, h1))

scenes.say: Your turn. Alice and Bob both pick the password hunter two. Does the users table store the same hash for both? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Alice and Bob both pick `hunter2`. Same stored hash?

scenes.head: Three ways to store a password
scenes.say: No. Each user gets a fresh salt, so the hashes differ. Plain text leaks everything the moment the database leaks. A plain fast hash lets attackers guess billions a second on a graphics card. B crypt is slow on purpose. Argon two is a modern alternative.
rows: slow on purpose, unique per user

scenes.say: That answers our problem. A slow salted hash means a leak reveals no passwords.

scenes.title: How does the server know it's you?
scenes.statement: After login, every request must prove who is calling, without sending the password again.

example.input: a request carrying a cookie or token

scenes.say: Next problem. After login, every request must prove who is calling, without the password. For example, a request with a cookie. We want the server to know it is user forty two.

scenes.head: A coat check ticket
scenes.say: Every request must prove who you are. Think of a coat check. You hand in your coat: that's logging in. You get a ticket: a session id, in a cookie. Each visit, you show the ticket. The clerk fetches your coat: the server finds user forty two.

scenes.head: A session lookup
scenes.say: Request one: the browser sends cookie abc nine. The server asks the session store: who is abc nine? The store answers, user forty two. Now the server knows who's calling. To log out, the server deletes the row. The ticket stops working at once.

scenes.head: A JWT is readable
scenes.say: Now the other way. A J W T needs no store. It has three parts joined by dots: header, payload, signature. Here's one for user forty two. Anyone can decode the payload. It prints sub forty two and an expiry.

panels.code:
tok = jwt.encode({"sub": "42", "exp": 1893456000}, KEY, "HS256")
head, body, sig = tok.split(".")
print(json.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(body + "==")))

scenes.head: Readable, but not editable
scenes.say: So can a user edit it? Change sub from forty two to one, keep the old signature, and verify. Rejected: the signature no longer matches. Signed, not secret.
Your turn. A token lasts one hour. The user logs out at minute five, but someone copied the token. At minute ten, does it still work? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: JWT valid 1 hour. Logout at minute 5. Copied token at minute 10?

scenes.head: Session vs JWT
scenes.say: Still accepted. Valid signature, expiry not reached, no list on the server. Where state lives: sessions keep it on the server, JWTs in the token. Logout: a session dies instantly. A JWT lives until it expires. Scaling: sessions need a shared store. Any server can verify a JWT. Size: a cookie is tiny, a JWT is bigger.
rows: on the server: id to user

scenes.head: Where does the token live?
scenes.say: Where does the browser keep it? Not in local storage: an injected script can read it. Use an HttpOnly, Secure cookie: scripts can't read it. And never put secrets in a JWT. Anyone can decode it.
rows: any injected script can read it
scripts can't read it; HTTPS only

scenes.say: That answers it. A session id or a signed token tells the server who is calling.

scenes.title: How do we log in with Google?
scenes.statement: Let people sign in with Google while the app never sees their Google password.

example.output: the app learns who you are, nothing more

scenes.say: Next problem. Sign in with Google, but our app never sees the password. For example, one click on log in with Google. We want the app to learn who you are, nothing more.

scenes.head: A valet key
scenes.say: Log in with Google. The app wants to know who you are, not your Google password. Think of a valet key. It starts the car but can't open the trunk. OAuth gives the app a limited key, never the master key.

scenes.head: OAuth in four arrows
scenes.say: Here's the dance. One: the app redirects you to Google. Two: you log in at Google and approve. Three: Google sends you back with a short lived code. Four: the app's server swaps the code for a token, using a secret only it knows. Your password never left Google.
Your turn. The code travels through the browser's address bar. A thief copies it. Is the code alone enough to get your token? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: A thief copies the short lived code. Enough to get the token?

scenes.head: A stolen code is not enough
scenes.say: No. The swap needs the app's secret, and only the app's server has it. The thief arrives with a code and no secret, and Google says no. That's why the code goes through the browser, but the token never does.

scenes.head: Authn vs authz
scenes.say: Now two words people mix up. Authentication asks: who are you? Failing it is four oh one. Authorization asks: what may you do? Failing that is four oh three.
That answers it. OAuth shows the app who you are, without your password.

scenes.title: How do we stop one client flooding?
scenes.statement: We know it's user 42. Now limit how much they may call: bursts are fine, floods are not.
scenes.say: Next problem. We know it's user forty two. Now limit how much they may call. For example, fifteen requests at once. We want ten to pass and five to get four twenty nine.

scenes.head: From who to how much
scenes.say: Now the server knows who's calling: user forty two. Next question: how much may they call? Picture an arcade coin jar. Each game costs one coin. The jar refills one coin a second, never above ten.

scenes.head: Fifteen requests, ten tokens
scenes.say: The token says sub forty two, so that's the key: one bucket per user. User forty two sends a burst of fifteen requests in one second. Each takes a token. Ten tokens, ten requests pass. The last five are rejected with four twenty nine.

scenes.head: The whole algorithm
scenes.say: The code needs no timer. We store the tokens, and the time of the last request. Each request, we compute how many tokens were earned since then, never above capacity. At least one? Spend it and say yes. Otherwise no. Constant time, constant memory per user.

scenes.head: Fifteen at once
scenes.say: Now run it. Capacity ten, one token a second. Fifteen requests at the same instant. Count the passes. Ten pass, five fail. One second later, a token is back. In real code, now comes from the clock.

panels.code:
b = TokenBucket(rate=1, cap=10)
passed = 0
for i in range(15):
    if b.allow(0): passed += 1
print(passed, 15 - passed)
print(b.allow(1))

scenes.say: Your turn. The bucket is empty after the burst. Three seconds pass. Five more requests arrive together. How many pass? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Empty bucket, refill 1 per second. 3 s later, 5 requests arrive. Passes?

scenes.head: Five requests, three seconds later
scenes.say: Three. Three seconds earned three tokens. Refill sets the long run speed. Of five requests, three pass and two get four twenty nine.
That answers it. A bucket per user lets ten through and rejects five.

scenes.title: One limit across many servers
scenes.statement: Two servers each count requests. How do we enforce one limit for the user across both?
scenes.say: Last problem. Two servers each count requests. For example, a limit of ten, and twenty requests split across them. We want only ten to pass in total.

scenes.head: Three algorithms, one catch each
scenes.say: Other ways exist. A fixed window counts per minute, so bursts can double at the edge. Sliding window avoids that, at a memory cost. Token bucket allows bursts up to capacity, then holds the average.
rows: double burst at the window edge

scenes.say: Your turn. You run two app servers, each with its own local bucket of ten. One client sends twenty requests, ten to each server. How many pass? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: 2 servers, local bucket of 10 each. 20 requests, 10 per server. Pass?

scenes.head: Local buckets leak
scenes.say: Twenty. Each server sees ten requests and its own full bucket, so everything passes. The limit was ten. The client got twenty. The fix is one shared bucket in Redis, a fast shared store, with a key per user. Both servers ask Redis. The read, refill and spend must be one atomic step, so a small Lua script, run inside Redis, does it.

scenes.head: What the client sees
scenes.say: Reject with four twenty nine. Add a Retry After header, so clients know when to come back. Two classic mistakes: counting in local memory, and a non atomic read then write. Capacity sets the burst. Refill sets the average.
That answers it. One shared Redis bucket enforces a single limit across servers.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Sessions versus JWT? Sessions keep state on the server. A JWT carries it, signed. Passwords? A slow salted hash: b crypt or Argon two. OAuth? Redirect, consent, code, token: the app never sees your password. Authn versus authz? Who you are, versus what you may do. Token storage? An HttpOnly cookie.
rows: who you are vs what you may do

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Token bucket? Refills at a fixed rate, each request spends one. Burst versus steady? Capacity sets the burst, refill sets the average. Many servers? Shared Redis, atomic Lua script, key per user. Status code? Four twenty nine, with Retry After. Mistake? Local counters, or a non atomic read then write.
rows: refills steadily, each request spends one
shared Redis, atomic Lua, key per user

scenes.head: Try this tonight
scenes.say: Try three things. Hash the same password twice with bcrypt, and compare the hashes. Decode a token's payload, forge the subject, and watch verification fail. Then write the bucket, and send fifteen requests at once.
So say this. Store passwords as slow salted hashes. A J W T is signed, not secret, and sessions revoke faster. Rate limit with a token bucket per user: capacity is the burst.
lines: Passwords: slow, salted hash. Never store them.
A JWT is signed, not secret. Sessions revoke fast.
One bucket per user: capacity = burst.
